definitions.definition: Multipurpose, programmable device that incorporates the CPU of a computer on a single IC and processes digital data according to instructions stored in memory.
8086 architecture in which the BIU fetches instructions while the EU executes them, so the two operations overlap.
Part of the 8086 that decodes and executes instructions; contains ALU, flag register, instruction decoder and general-purpose, pointer and index registers.
Part of the 8086 that handles data and address transfers with memory and I/O devices, computes physical addresses and prefetches instructions.
Six-byte FIFO register set inside the BIU that stores prefetched instructions for the EU.
16-bit status register that reflects ALU computation results and holds nine active bits, six conditional and three control.
Set when addition generates a carry out of the MSB or subtraction requires a borrow.
Set to 1 when the result of an operation is zero and cleared when the result is nonzero.
Copies the MSB of the result, indicating whether the result is positive or negative.
Set when the carry entering the MSB differs from the carry leaving it, meaning the result exceeds available capacity.
CS, DS, ES and SS: 16-bit units holding the starting addresses of code, data, extra and stack memory areas.
20-bit actual address of a memory location, computed by a dedicated adder in the BIU from the segment and offset registers.
8086 configuration with MN/MX = 1 in which a single microprocessor generates all control signals itself.
8086 configuration with MN/MX = 0 in which status signals S0–S2 are decoded by an external bus controller.
Specifies a way of locating the data or operands that an instruction operates on.
Mode in which the operand is part of the instruction itself, stored in successive bytes; e.g. MOV AX, 0005H.
Mode in which the operand is stored in a register and referred to using that register; e.g. MOV AX, BX.
Mode in which the memory address of the operand is specified directly in the instruction; e.g. MOV AX, [5000].
Mode in which the operand address is stored indirectly in an offset register such as BX, SI or DI; e.g. MOV AX, [BX].
Mode in which the physical address is formed by adding base register contents (BX/BP) to index register contents (SI/DI).
Instruction that places the contents of a register or memory location onto the stack; SP is decremented by 2.
Copies a word from the top of the stack into the specified register or memory location; SP is incremented by 2.
Subtracts the source operand from the destination only to update flags; the result is not stored anywhere.
Unsigned multiplication of AL (or AX) with a byte (or word) operand; the result goes to AX (or DX:AX).
Software interrupt instruction with a type number 0–255 that calls the corresponding service routine; type 3 is the break-point interrupt.
Executes a labelled block of code the number of times specified in CX, decrementing CX automatically at each iteration.
Predefined alphabetical strings (e.g. ASSUME, ORG, EQU) that give hints to the assembler to understand the program correctly.
Group of repetitive instructions stored as a separate program in memory and invoked with CALL; near if in the same code segment, far otherwise.
Group of repetitive instructions defined by assembler directives whose machine code is generated each time it is invoked, hence uses more memory.
Programmable peripheral interface used to control communication between the microprocessor and I/O devices through programmable ports A, B and C.
Bit set/reset mode used to set or reset individual bits of port C; selected when control word bit D7 = 0.
Simple I/O mode that provides plain input/output capability for all three ports, with outputs latched and no handshaking.
Strobed I/O mode in which handshake signals taken from port C lines control the I/O action of ports A and B.
Strobed bidirectional mode in which data is transmitted and received on 8-bit port A with handshaking on PC3–PC7.
8-bit CMOS successive-approximation ADC with an internal 3:8 analog multiplexer for eight analog inputs; conversion delay 100 µs at a 640 kHz clock.
16-pin 8-bit multiplying digital-to-analog converter containing an R-2R ladder network for D-A conversion.
Device for accurate position control of rotating shafts that rotates in steps when a pulse sequence is applied to its windings.
Making the processor wait (~10 ms) for a pressed key's mechanical bounce to settle, so a single press is not read as multiple presses.
Programmable interrupt controller that manages interrupt requests with masking and programmed priority; 8 interrupt inputs per chip, cascadable up to 64.
A computer present in a single integrated circuit dedicated to one task, containing processor, memory and programmable I/O peripherals on one chip.
8-bit microcontroller with 4 KB on-chip ROM, 128 bytes RAM, four 8-bit I/O ports, two 16-bit timers/counters and one serial port.
Four 8-bit bidirectional ports P0–P3; P0 needs external pull-ups and multiplexes low address/data, P2 supplies the high address byte, P3 bits have alternate functions.
Program Store Enable — active-low output pin that acts as the read strobe for external program memory.
Pin tied low to fetch code from external ROM as in the 8031, and connected to VCC in the 8051 to use internal ROM.
Four groups of eight working locations R0–R7 in internal RAM, selected by PSW bits RS1 and RS0, permitting fast context switching in ISRs.
16-bit data pointer register of the 8051 used to address external data memory.
Timer mode register that selects timer or counter operation and the operating mode (0–3) for timer 0 and timer 1.
Timer control register holding run-control bits TR0/TR1, overflow flags TF0/TF1 and external-interrupt type/edge bits IT0, IT1, IE0, IE1.
8051 unit through which each interrupt source, all disabled after reset, can be turned on or off separately.
Display with a built-in refreshing controller that can show numbers, characters and graphics, relieving the CPU of the refresh task.
Rate at which data is sent over a serial link, in bits per second; at 9600 bits per second one bit takes 0.104 ms.
Serial communication in which transmitter and receiver are synchronized by a common clock; a sync character is sent before the data.
Serial communication using independent clocks, with each byte framed by a start bit, data bits and a stop bit.
EIA serial I/O interfacing standard in which logic 1 is −3 to −25 V and logic 0 is +3 to +25 V.
IC commonly used to convert the TTL logic levels of a microcontroller to RS232 voltage levels.
Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter — hardware that translates data between parallel and serial forms.
Serial buffer register of the 8051; two registers share the name — one write-only for transmission and one read-only for reception.
Serial control register holding the mode-selection bits, REN and the serial-port interrupt flags TI and RI.
Power control register; its SMOD bit modifies the baud rate of serial communication, while other bits set power-down and idle modes.
